notes.front: What is Kanban, as the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams defines it?
notes.back: A strategy for optimising the flow of value through a process, using a visual, work-in-progress-limited pull system.
notes.explanation: The flow of value is what Kanban sets out to optimise; the visual, limited, pull-based system is how.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Definition of Kanban”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Kanban (n): a strategy for optimizing the flow of value through a process that uses a visual, workin-progress limited pull system.
notes.example: Like a café’s order rail: everyone can see the waiting orders, and a barista takes the next one only when free.

notes.front: In the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams, what is flow?
notes.back: The movement of value throughout the product development system.
notes.explanation: Flow is central to the definition of Kanban.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Flow and Empiricism”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Central to the definition of Kanban is the concept of flow. Flow is the movement of value throughout the product development system.
notes.example: Like parcels moving through a sorting depot: what matters is how smoothly each gets from arrival to dispatch.

notes.front: What is Work in Progress (WIP), as a flow metric?
notes.back: The number of work items started but not finished.
notes.explanation: It is one of the four basic metrics of flow that Scrum Teams using Kanban need to track.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Work in Progress (WIP): The number of work items started but not finished.
notes.example: Like the number of library books you have borrowed and not yet returned.

notes.front: What is Cycle Time?
notes.back: The elapsed time between when a work item starts and when it finishes.
notes.explanation: It is measured from start to finish, so it describes items that have finished.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Cycle Time: The amount of elapsed time between when a work item starts and when a work item finishes.
notes.example: Like the days between a repair shop starting on your bicycle and handing it back to you.

notes.front: What is Work Item Age?
notes.back: The time between when a work item started and now; it applies only to items still in progress.
notes.explanation: It shows how long unfinished work has already been under way.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Work Item Age: The amount of time between when a work item started and the current time. This applies only to items that are still in progress.
notes.example: Like checking how long a pot has been on the stove while it is still cooking.

notes.front: What is Throughput?
notes.back: The number of work items finished per unit of time.
notes.explanation: It counts items finished, not items started or effort spent.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Throughput: The number of work items finished per unit of time.
notes.example: Like a bakery counting the loaves that come out of the oven each hour.

notes.front: What is Little’s Law, in the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams?
notes.back: A guideline: for a given throughput, the more you work on at once, the longer things take to finish (on average).
notes.explanation: The guide calls it a key tenet governing flow theory.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Little’s Law – The Key to Governing Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: A key tenet governing flow theory is Little’s Law, which is a guideline that establishes the following relationship: Little’s Law reveals that in general, for a given process with a given throughput, the more things that you work on at any given time (on average), the longer it is going to take to finish those things (on average).
notes.example: Like a supermarket with a fixed number of tills: the more trolleys queue, the longer the average shopper waits.

notes.front: What is a Scrum Team’s Definition of Workflow?
notes.back: The Scrum Team members’ explicit understanding of their policies for following the Kanban practices.
notes.explanation: This shared understanding improves transparency and enables self-management.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Definition of Workflow”, p. 5
notes.evidence: The four Kanban practices are enabled by the Scrum Team’s Definition of Workflow. This definition represents the Scrum Team members’ explicit understanding of what their policies are for following the Kanban practices. This shared understanding improves transparency and enables self-management.
notes.example: Like a kitchen’s posted house rules for how orders move from ticket to table, agreed by the cooks themselves.

notes.front: What is a Kanban board for, in the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams?
notes.back: It is how the Scrum Team visualises its Workflow and makes it transparent.
notes.explanation: Its configuration should prompt the right conversations at the right time and proactively suggest opportunities for improvement.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Visualization of the Workflow – the Kanban Board”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Visualization using the Kanban board is the way the Scrum Team makes its Workflow transparent. The board's configuration should prompt the right conversations at the right time and proactively suggest opportunities for improvement.
notes.example: Like a wall of sticky notes in columns such as “Doing”, “Testing” and “Done” that the whole team can read at a glance.

notes.front: What is a pull system, in Kanban?
notes.back: A system in which the team starts (pulls) an item only when it is clear that it has the capacity to do so.
notes.explanation: The guide says creating one is the primary effect of limiting WIP.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Limiting Work in Progress (WIP)”, p. 5
notes.evidence: The primary effect of limiting WIP is that it creates a pull system. It is called a pull system because the team starts work (i.e. pulls) on an item only when it is clear that it has the capacity to do so.
notes.example: Like a taxi rank where the next taxi takes a passenger only once it is free.

notes.front: What is a Service Level Expectation (SLE)?
notes.back: A forecast of how long it should take a given item to flow from start to finish within the Scrum Team’s Workflow.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Team uses it to find active flow issues, and to inspect and adapt when flow falls short of that expectation.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Service Level Expectation (SLE)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A service level expectation (SLE) forecasts how long it should take a given item to flow from start to finish within the Scrum Team’s Workflow. The Scrum Team uses its SLE to find active flow issues and to inspect and adapt in cases of falling below those expectations.
notes.example: Like a dry cleaner telling customers that most orders are ready within three days.

notes.front: What can a cumulative flow diagram visualise for a Scrum Team?
notes.back: Its WIP, approximate average Cycle Time and average Throughput.
notes.explanation: The guide says using one for this “can be valuable”; it does not require it.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Using a cumulative flow diagram to visualize a Scrum Team’s WIP, approximate average Cycle Time and average Throughput can be valuable.
notes.example: Like a chart of stacked coloured bands, one per board column, that widen or narrow day by day.

notes.front: Does the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams replace any part of the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: No. It is designed to enhance and expand Scrum’s practices; the Scrum Guide applies in its entirety.
notes.explanation: The guide assumes its reader is already operating a process using the Scrum framework.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Relation to the Scrum Guide”, p. 3
notes.evidence: This guide does not replace or discount any part of The Scrum Guide. It is designed to enhance and expand the practices of Scrum. This guide assumes the reader is operating a process using the Scrum framework. Therefore, The Scrum Guide applies in its entirety.

notes.front: When can Scrum Teams add Kanban practices?
notes.back: Whether they are just starting to use Scrum or have been using it all along.
notes.explanation: The guide presents Kanban’s flow-based perspective as able to enhance and complement Scrum.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Purpose”, p. 3
notes.evidence: The flow-based perspective of Kanban can enhance and complement the Scrum framework and its implementation. Teams can add complementary Kanban practices whether they are just starting to use Scrum or have been using it all along.

notes.front: By improving which three qualities of a process does Kanban optimise flow?
notes.back: Its overall efficiency, effectiveness and predictability.
notes.explanation: These improvements serve flow, the movement of value through the system.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Flow and Empiricism”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Kanban optimizes flow by improving the overall efficiency, effectiveness, and predictability of a process.

notes.front: According to the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams, what is key to empirical process control, and what can it also be called?
notes.back: The frequency of the transparency, inspection and adaptation cycle: the Cycle Time through the feedback loop.
notes.explanation: Seen this way, a faster feedback loop means more frequent inspection and adaptation.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Flow and Empiricism”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Key to empirical process control is the frequency of the transparency, inspection, and adaptation cycle - which we can also describe as the Cycle Time through the feedback loop.

notes.front: How many basic metrics of flow does the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams say Scrum Teams using Kanban need to track?
notes.back: Four.
notes.explanation: They are WIP, Cycle Time, Work Item Age and Throughput.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: The four basic metrics of flow that Scrum Teams using Kanban need to track are as follows:

notes.front: Is the WIP metric the same thing as the policies a Scrum Team uses to limit WIP?
notes.back: No. The guide notes a difference between the two.
notes.explanation: The metric gives transparency about progress in reducing WIP; the policies are what set the limit.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: The team can use the WIP metric to provide transparency about their progress towards reducing their WIP and improving their flow. Note that there is a difference between the WIP metric and the policies a Scrum Team uses to limit WIP.

notes.front: How does Cycle Time differ from Work Item Age?
notes.back: Cycle Time runs from start to finish of a work item; Work Item Age runs from start to now, for items still in progress.
notes.explanation: One describes finished work, the other unfinished work.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Cycle Time: The amount of elapsed time between when a work item starts and when a work item finishes. Work Item Age: The amount of time between when a work item started and the current time. This applies only to items that are still in progress.

notes.front: What relationship does the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams give for Little’s Law?
notes.back: Average Cycle Time = average work in progress ÷ average Throughput.
notes.explanation: With throughput unchanged, more work in progress means a longer average time to finish.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Little’s Law – The Key to Governing Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Little’s Law reveals that in general, for a given process with a given throughput, the more things that you work on at any given time (on average), the longer it is going to take to finish those things (on average).

image.alt: An equation: average cycle time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput.
image.credit: Scrum.org, The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Little’s Law – The Key to Governing Flow”, p. 4

notes.front: If Cycle Times are too long, what is the first action Scrum Teams should consider?
notes.back: Lowering WIP.
notes.explanation: Most of the other elements of Kanban are built on the relationship between WIP and Cycle Time.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Little’s Law – The Key to Governing Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: If cycle times are too long, the first action Scrum Teams should consider is lowering WIP. Most of the other elements of Kanban are built upon the relationship between WIP and Cycle Time.

notes.front: What does Little’s Law show about flow theory and empiricism?
notes.back: Flow theory relies on empiricism: flow metrics and data give transparency into past flow and inform inspection and adaptation experiments.
notes.explanation: Flow metrics are the evidence the team inspects before adapting.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Little’s Law – The Key to Governing Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Little's Law also shows us how flow theory relies on empiricism by using flow metrics and data to gain transparency into historical flow and then using that data to inform flow inspection and adaptation experiments.

notes.front: Which of the four Kanban practices makes the Scrum Team’s Workflow transparent?
notes.back: Visualisation of the Workflow, using the Kanban board.
notes.explanation: The board’s configuration should prompt the right conversations and suggest opportunities for improvement.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Visualization of the Workflow – the Kanban Board”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Visualization using the Kanban board is the way the Scrum Team makes its Workflow transparent. The board's configuration should prompt the right conversations at the right time and proactively suggest opportunities for improvement.

notes.front: Which Kanban practice does the guide call necessary to achieve flow, but not sufficient on its own?
notes.back: Limiting Work in Progress (WIP).
notes.explanation: Limiting WIP helps flow, but the guide adds another practice to establish it.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Active Management of Work Items in Progress”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Limiting WIP is necessary to achieve flow, but it alone is not sufficient.

notes.front: Which Kanban practice does the guide call the third practice to establish flow, carried out by the Scrum Team within the Sprint?
notes.back: Active management of work items in progress.
notes.explanation: Within the Sprint it can take several forms, and the guide’s list of them is open.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Active Management of Work Items in Progress”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The third practice to establish flow is the active management of work items in progress. Within the Sprint, this management by the Scrum Team can take several forms, including but not limited to the following:

notes.front: Which Kanban practice does the Scrum Team carry out through the existing Scrum events?
notes.back: Inspecting and adapting its Definition of Workflow.
notes.explanation: Doing so helps improve empiricism and optimise the value the Scrum Team delivers.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Inspect and Adapt the Definition of Workflow”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team uses the existing Scrum events to inspect and adapt its Definition of Workflow, thereby helping to improve empiricism and optimizing the value the Scrum Team delivers.

notes.front: May a Scrum Team’s Definition of Workflow cover flow outside the Sprint?
notes.back: Yes. Its scope may span beyond the Sprint and the Sprint Backlog.
notes.explanation: It may encompass flow inside and/or outside the Sprint.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Definition of Workflow”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Note that the scope of the Definition of Workflow may span beyond the Sprint and the Sprint Backlog. For instance, a Scrum Team's Definition of Workflow may encompass flow inside and/or outside of the Sprint.

notes.front: Who is accountable for creating and adapting the Definition of Workflow?
notes.back: The relevant roles on the Scrum Team, as described in the Scrum Guide.
notes.explanation: The Kanban guide places this inside the Scrum Team, using the Scrum Guide’s accountabilities.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Definition of Workflow”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Creating and adapting the Definition of Workflow is the accountability of the relevant roles on the Scrum Team as described in the Scrum Guide.

notes.front: Who outside the Scrum Team should tell the team how to define its Workflow?
notes.back: No one.
notes.explanation: Creating and adapting the Definition of Workflow is the accountability of roles on the Scrum Team.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Definition of Workflow”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Creating and adapting the Definition of Workflow is the accountability of the relevant roles on the Scrum Team as described in the Scrum Guide. No one outside of the Scrum Team should tell the Scrum Team how to define their Workflow.

notes.front: What should Kanban visualisation show about when work begins and ends?
notes.back: Defined points at which the Scrum Team considers work to have started and to have finished.
notes.explanation: It is the first of five things the guide says visualisation should include.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Visualization of the Workflow – the Kanban Board”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Visualization should include the following: • • • • • Defined points at which the Scrum Team considers work to have started and to have finished.

notes.front: In Kanban visualisation, what are the work items, and what are they most likely to be?
notes.back: The individual units of value flowing through the team’s system; most likely Product Backlog items.
notes.explanation: The value may be stakeholder value, knowledge value or process improvement value.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Visualization of the Workflow – the Kanban Board”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A definition of the work items - the individual units of value (stakeholder value, knowledge value, process improvement value) that are flowing through the Scrum Team's system (most likely Product Backlog items (PBIs)).

notes.front: In Kanban visualisation, how many active workflow states must there be at minimum?
notes.back: At least one.
notes.explanation: The workflow states are those the work items flow through from start to finish.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Visualization of the Workflow – the Kanban Board”, p. 5
notes.evidence: A definition of the workflow states that the work items flow through from start to finish (of which there must be at least one active state).

notes.front: What may a team’s explicit policies about how work flows through each state include?
notes.back: Items from the Scrum Team’s Definition of Done, and pull policies between stages.
notes.explanation: The guide says “may include”: these are possible contents, not required ones.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Visualization of the Workflow – the Kanban Board”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Explicit policies about how work flows through each state (which may include items from a Scrum Team's Definition of Done and pull policies between stages).

notes.front: Which WIP-related item should Kanban visualisation include?
notes.back: Policies for limiting WIP.
notes.explanation: It completes the guide’s list of five things visualisation should include.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Visualization of the Workflow – the Kanban Board”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Policies for limiting Work in Progress (WIP).

notes.front: How must a Scrum Team using Kanban limit WIP?
notes.back: Explicitly, in whatever way it sees fit, but it should stick to the limit once established.
notes.explanation: The guide leaves the method to the team but asks it to keep to the limit it sets.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Limiting Work in Progress (WIP)”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Scrum Teams using Kanban must explicitly limit the number of these work items in progress. A Scrum Team can explicitly limit WIP however they see fit but should stick to that limit once established.

notes.front: In a pull system, what is the signal to start new work?
notes.back: WIP dropping below the defined limit.
notes.explanation: Work starts because capacity has freed up.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Limiting Work in Progress (WIP)”, p. 5
notes.evidence: When the WIP drops below the defined limit, that is the signal to start new work.

notes.front: How does a pull system differ from a push system?
notes.back: A pull system starts work only when there is clear capacity; a push system starts work on an item whenever it is requested.
notes.explanation: A WIP limit is what decides when a pull system may start new work.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Limiting Work in Progress (WIP)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: different from a push system, which demands that work starts on an item whenever it is requested.

notes.front: Besides helping flow, what are two things limiting WIP improves for a Scrum Team?
notes.back: Any two of: self-management, focus, commitment, collaboration.
notes.explanation: The guide lists these alongside better flow as effects of limiting WIP.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Active Management of Work Items in Progress”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Limiting WIP helps flow and improves the Scrum Team's self-management, focus, commitment, and collaboration.

notes.front: Which form of active management keeps the rate of work entering the Workflow in line with the rate it leaves?
notes.back: Pulling work items into the Workflow at about the same rate that they leave it.
notes.explanation: The guide’s forms of active management are “including but not limited to” its list.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Active Management of Work Items in Progress”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Making sure that work items are only pulled into the Workflow at about the same rate that they leave the Workflow.

notes.front: Which form of active management deals with work items sitting in progress too long?
notes.back: Ensuring work items aren’t left to age unnecessarily.
notes.explanation: Work Item Age is the flow metric that shows how long an item has been in progress.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Active Management of Work Items in Progress”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Ensuring work items aren't left to age unnecessarily.

notes.front: Which form of active management concerns blocked or queued items and those running slower than expected?
notes.back: Responding quickly to them, including items exceeding the team’s expected Cycle Time levels.
notes.explanation: The guide points to the SLE for judging what counts as too slow.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Active Management of Work Items in Progress”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Responding quickly to blocked or queued work items as well those that are exceeding the team’s expected Cycle Time levels (See Service Level Expectation - SLE).

notes.front: What are the two parts of an SLE?
notes.back: A range of elapsed days, and a probability for that period (e.g. 85% of items finished in eight days or less).
notes.explanation: The probability says how often items are expected to finish within the range.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Service Level Expectation (SLE)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The SLE itself has two parts: a range of elapsed days and a probability associated with that period (e.g., 85% of work items should be finished in eight days or less).

notes.front: What should an SLE be based on, and what if there is no data yet?
notes.back: The team’s historical Cycle Time; without history, a best guess, inspected and adapted once enough data exists.
notes.explanation: Once calculated, the SLE should be made transparent.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Service Level Expectation (SLE)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The SLE should be based on the Scrum Team's historical Cycle Time, and once calculated, the Scrum Team should make it transparent. If no historical Cycle Time data exists, the Scrum Team should make its best guess and then inspect and adapt once there is enough historical data to do a proper SLE calculation.

notes.front: What are two how-we-work policy changes the guide says can have a dramatic impact?
notes.back: Any two of: adjusting WIP limits, adjusting SLEs, changing the batch size.
notes.explanation: Such policies, part of the Definition of Workflow, can directly address an impediment.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Inspect and Adapt the Definition of Workflow”, p. 6
notes.evidence: How-we-work policies - these can directly address an impediment. For example, adjusting WIP limits and SLEs or changing the batch size (how often items are pulled between states) can have a dramatic impact.

notes.front: Does using Kanban with Scrum require any events beyond those in the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Instead, bringing a flow-based perspective and metrics into Scrum’s events strengthens its empirical approach.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Flow-Based Events”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Kanban in a Scrum context does not require any additional events to those outlined in The Scrum Guide. However, using a flow-based perspective and metrics in Scrum’s events strengthens Scrum’s empirical approach.

notes.front: Do Kanban practices remove the need for Scrum’s Sprint?
notes.back: No. The Sprint and its events still give opportunities to inspect and adapt both product and process.
notes.explanation: Kanban practices complement the Sprint rather than replacing it.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Sprint”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The Kanban complementary practices don’t invalidate the need for Scrum’s Sprint. The Sprint and its events provide opportunities for inspection and adaptation of both product and process.

notes.front: Can Scrum Teams deliver value only once per Sprint?
notes.back: No; that is a common misconception. They must deliver value at least once per Sprint.
notes.explanation: Once per Sprint is the minimum, not the limit.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Sprint”, p. 7
notes.evidence: It’s a common misconception that teams can only deliver value once per Sprint. In fact, they must deliver value at least once per Sprint.

notes.front: What does Scrum’s empiricism encourage about Increments within a Sprint, according to the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams?
notes.back: Creating multiple valuable Increments during the Sprint, to enable fast inspect-and-adapt feedback loops.
notes.explanation: One valuable, useful Increment per Sprint is only the minimum Scrum requires.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Increment”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Scrum requires the team to create (at minimum) a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint. Scrum’s empiricism encourages the creation of multiple valuable increments during the Sprint to enable fast inspect and adapt feedback loops.

notes.front: In flow-based Sprint Planning, what can reviewing historical Throughput help a Scrum Team understand?
notes.back: Its capacity for the next Sprint.
notes.explanation: Flow metrics serve as an aid in developing the Sprint Backlog.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Sprint Planning”, p. 7
notes.evidence: A flow-based Sprint Planning meeting uses flow metrics as an aid for developing the Sprint Backlog. Reviewing historical throughput can help a Scrum Team understand their capacity for the next Sprint.

notes.front: Where does a flow-based Daily Scrum take place, and what does it focus on?
notes.back: Around the Kanban board, on where flow is lacking and what the Developers can do to get it back.
notes.explanation: The goal of the Daily Scrum stays as the Scrum Guide sets it; only the focus of the conversation shifts.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Daily Scrum”, p. 7
notes.evidence: While the goal of the Daily Scrum remains the same as outlined in The Scrum Guide, the meeting itself takes place around the Kanban board and focuses on where flow is lacking and on what actions the Developers can take to get it back.

notes.front: What are two things to consider during a flow-based Daily Scrum?
notes.back: Any two, among others: blocked items; work flowing slower than expected; each item’s Work Item Age; items at or past their SLE.
notes.explanation: The guide’s list also covers factors not on the board, new learning and broken WIP limits.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Daily Scrum”, p. 7
notes.evidence: What work items are blocked and what can be done to get them unblocked? What work is flowing slower than expected? What is the Work Item Age of each item in progress? What work items have violated or are about to violate their SLE

notes.front: At the Sprint Review, how can reviewing Throughput help the Product Owner?
notes.back: It can add information when the Product Owner discusses likely delivery dates.
notes.explanation: Inspecting flow metrics can open new conversations about progress toward the Product Goal.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Sprint Review”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Inspecting Kanban flow metrics as part of the review can create opportunities for new conversations about monitoring progress towards the Product Goal. Reviewing Throughput can provide additional information when the Product Owner discusses likely delivery dates.

notes.front: What does a flow-based Sprint Retrospective add?
notes.back: Inspection of flow metrics and analytics, and inspecting and adapting the Definition of Workflow for the next Sprint.
notes.explanation: The metrics help the Scrum Team decide what improvements to make to its processes.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: A flow-based Sprint Retrospective adds the inspection of flow metrics and analytics to help determine what improvements the Scrum Team can make to its processes. The Scrum Team using Kanban also inspects and adapts the Definition of Workflow to optimize the flow in the next Sprint.

notes.front: When may a Scrum Team change its Definition of Workflow, and what does making changes at the Sprint Retrospective bring?
notes.back: At any time; changes at the Retrospective’s regular cadence reduce complexity and improve focus, commitment and transparency.
notes.explanation: The guide notes such changes have a material impact on how the Scrum Team performs.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: Similarly, changes to a Scrum Team’s Definition of Workflow may happen at any time. Because these changes will have a material impact on how the Scrum Team performs, changes made during the regular cadence provided by the Sprint Retrospective event will reduce complexity and improve focus, commitment and transparency.

notes.front: A team counts 14 items on its board that have been started but are not yet finished. Which flow metric is this?
notes.back: B) Work in Progress (WIP)
notes.explanation: A count of items started but not finished is the definition of WIP.
notes.choices:
A) Throughput
B) Work in Progress (WIP)
C) Cycle Time
D) Work Item Age
notes.choicesExplained: A counts items finished per unit of time. C is the time from start to finish of an item. D is how long one unfinished item has been in progress.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Work in Progress (WIP): The number of work items started but not finished.

notes.front: A work item started on a Monday and was finished ten days later, on the Thursday of the following week. Which flow metric do those ten days describe?
notes.back: D) Cycle Time
notes.explanation: Elapsed time from start to finish of a work item is Cycle Time.
notes.choices:
A) Work Item Age
B) Work in Progress (WIP)
C) Throughput
D) Cycle Time
notes.choicesExplained: A applies only to items still in progress. C counts finished items per unit of time. B counts items, not time.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Cycle Time: The amount of elapsed time between when a work item starts and when a work item finishes. Work Item Age: The amount of time between when a work item started and the current time. This applies only to items that are still in progress.

notes.front: At the Daily Scrum, one item has been in progress for nine days and is still not finished. Which flow metric is “nine days”?
notes.back: C) Work Item Age
notes.explanation: Time since an unfinished item started is its Work Item Age.
notes.choices:
A) Cycle Time
B) Throughput
C) Work Item Age
D) Service Level Expectation (SLE)
notes.choicesExplained: A needs the item to have finished. B counts finished items. D is a forecast for items, not a measurement of one item’s time so far.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Work Item Age: The amount of time between when a work item started and the current time. This applies only to items that are still in progress.

notes.front: Over its last four Sprints a team finished 12, 15, 11 and 14 items. Which flow metric are these numbers?
notes.back: B) Throughput
notes.explanation: Items finished per unit of time, here per Sprint, is Throughput.
notes.choices:
A) Work Item Age
B) Throughput
C) Cycle Time
D) Work in Progress (WIP)
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are times, not counts. D counts items started but unfinished at one moment, not items finished per period.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Basic Metrics of Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Throughput: The number of work items finished per unit of time.

notes.front: Over two months a team’s Cycle Times have doubled. Throughput is steady, and each Developer now has four items on the go. What should the Scrum Master first encourage the team to consider?
notes.back: C) Lowering WIP
notes.explanation: The Kanban guide names lowering WIP as the first action to consider when Cycle Times are too long.
notes.choices:
A) Starting more items so that more of them finish
B) Adding a daily status meeting with management
C) Lowering WIP
D) Making the Sprint longer
notes.choicesExplained: B adds an event Kanban with Scrum does not need. A raises WIP, which by Little’s Law lengthens Cycle Time. D does not touch the WIP that drives Cycle Time.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Little’s Law – The Key to Governing Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: If cycle times are too long, the first action Scrum Teams should consider is lowering WIP. Most of the other elements of Kanban are built upon the relationship between WIP and Cycle Time.

notes.front: A team’s Throughput stays the same, but the average number of items it works on at once doubles. By Little’s Law, what happens to the average Cycle Time?
notes.back: B) It gets longer
notes.explanation: For a given throughput, working on more at once makes things take longer to finish, on average.
notes.choices:
A) It gets shorter
B) It gets longer
C) It stays the same
D) It depends only on the size of the items
notes.choicesExplained: A and C contradict the relationship the guide gives. D ignores that, for a given throughput, WIP drives average Cycle Time.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Little’s Law – The Key to Governing Flow”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Little’s Law reveals that in general, for a given process with a given throughput, the more things that you work on at any given time (on average), the longer it is going to take to finish those things (on average).

notes.front: A department head sends a Scrum Team a mandatory board layout and WIP limits copied from another department. As Scrum Master, how do you respond?
notes.back: D) Explain that no one outside the Scrum Team should tell it how to define its Workflow; the team decides
notes.explanation: The Kanban guide keeps the Definition of Workflow with the Scrum Team.
notes.choices:
A) Adopt them as sent, since management sets how teams work
B) Adopt them, but keep the team’s old board alongside
C) Ask the Product Owner alone to redesign the Workflow
D) Explain that no one outside the Scrum Team should tell it how to define its Workflow; the team decides
notes.choicesExplained: A and B let an outsider define the team’s Workflow. C narrows an accountability the guide gives to the relevant roles on the Scrum Team.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Definition of Workflow”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Creating and adapting the Definition of Workflow is the accountability of the relevant roles on the Scrum Team as described in the Scrum Guide. No one outside of the Scrum Team should tell the Scrum Team how to define their Workflow.

notes.front: A team’s board has columns, but nobody agrees when an item counts as “started”, so its Cycle Time figures swing wildly. Which part of visualisation is missing?
notes.back: A) Defined points at which work is considered started and finished
notes.explanation: Cycle Time runs from when an item starts to when it finishes, so the start and finish points must be defined.
notes.choices:
A) Defined points at which work is considered started and finished
B) A definition of the work items
C) At least one active workflow state
D) Policies for limiting WIP
notes.choicesExplained: D, B and C are other parts of visualisation, but none of them fixes when an item’s clock starts.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Visualization of the Workflow – the Kanban Board”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Visualization should include the following: • • • • • Defined points at which the Scrum Team considers work to have started and to have finished.

notes.front: A stakeholder insists that a team start her request today, although the team is at its WIP limit. What does the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams point to?
notes.back: D) In a pull system, new work starts only when WIP drops below the limit; starting on request is a push system
notes.explanation: The guide contrasts a pull system, which waits for capacity, with a push system that starts work whenever asked.
notes.choices:
A) Start it, since WIP limits apply only to the Developers’ own ideas
B) Raise the WIP limit whenever a stakeholder asks
C) Start the request and pause the oldest item
D) In a pull system, new work starts only when WIP drops below the limit; starting on request is a push system
notes.choicesExplained: B abandons the limit the team should stick to. C and A start work on request, which is how a push system works.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Limiting Work in Progress (WIP)”, p. 5
notes.evidence: When the WIP drops below the defined limit, that is the signal to start new work.

notes.front: An item has been in progress for eleven days. The team’s SLE says 85% of items finish within eight days. What should the team do?
notes.back: B) Treat it as an active flow issue and respond quickly to get it finished
notes.explanation: The SLE exists to help the team find active flow issues such as this one, and to inspect and adapt.
notes.choices:
A) Change the SLE to twelve days straight away
B) Treat it as an active flow issue and respond quickly to get it finished
C) Leave it until the Sprint Review
D) Stop it and restart it from the beginning
notes.choicesExplained: A rewrites the forecast instead of using it. C delays the quick response active management calls for. D throws away work without dealing with the cause.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Service Level Expectation (SLE)”, p. 6
notes.evidence: A service level expectation (SLE) forecasts how long it should take a given item to flow from start to finish within the Scrum Team’s Workflow. The Scrum Team uses its SLE to find active flow issues and to inspect and adapt in cases of falling below those expectations.

notes.front: A team adopting Kanban proposes a new weekly “flow review” meeting, because “Kanban needs its own events”. What should the Scrum Master say?
notes.back: B) Kanban with Scrum needs no extra events; bring flow metrics into the existing Scrum events
notes.explanation: The guide says a flow-based perspective in Scrum’s own events strengthens its empirical approach.
notes.choices:
A) Agree: Kanban brings its own set of events
B) Kanban with Scrum needs no extra events; bring flow metrics into the existing Scrum events
C) Replace the Sprint Retrospective with the flow review
D) Replace the Daily Scrum with the flow review
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the guide requires no additional events. C and D drop Scrum events, which the Kanban guide does not replace.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Flow-Based Events”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Kanban in a Scrum context does not require any additional events to those outlined in The Scrum Guide. However, using a flow-based perspective and metrics in Scrum’s events strengthens Scrum’s empirical approach.

notes.front: A team that now releases continuously proposes dropping Sprints, because “with Kanban, flow makes them pointless”. How should the Scrum Master respond?
notes.back: B) Kanban practices don’t invalidate the Sprint; its events give inspection and adaptation of product and process
notes.explanation: The Kanban guide keeps the Sprint and uses its events as a feedback improvement loop.
notes.choices:
A) Agree: continuous flow replaces the Sprint
B) Kanban practices don’t invalidate the Sprint; its events give inspection and adaptation of product and process
C) Let the Product Owner decide whether Sprints are still needed
D) Keep the Sprint only for the Sprint Review
notes.choicesExplained: A contradicts the guide. D keeps one event but loses the others the Sprint contains. C hands over a choice the framework has already made.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Sprint”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The Kanban complementary practices don’t invalidate the need for Scrum’s Sprint. The Sprint and its events provide opportunities for inspection and adaptation of both product and process.

notes.front: A Product Owner says: “We can’t release mid-Sprint; value is delivered once per Sprint, at the Sprint Review.” What should the Scrum Master point out?
notes.back: C) That is a common misconception: teams must deliver value at least once per Sprint, and may do so more often
notes.explanation: The Kanban guide says once per Sprint is the minimum, not the only time value can be delivered.
notes.choices:
A) That is correct in Scrum
B) Mid-Sprint releases are allowed only with a Kanban board
C) That is a common misconception: teams must deliver value at least once per Sprint, and may do so more often
D) Mid-Sprint releases need the stakeholders’ approval at the Sprint Review
notes.choicesExplained: A repeats the misconception. B and D invent conditions the guide does not set.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “The Sprint”, p. 7
notes.evidence: It’s a common misconception that teams can only deliver value once per Sprint. In fact, they must deliver value at least once per Sprint.

notes.front: At a team’s Daily Scrum, each person reports what they did yesterday, while three items sit blocked on the board. How might a flow-based Daily Scrum change this?
notes.back: C) Hold it around the Kanban board and focus on where flow is lacking, such as the blocked items
notes.explanation: A flow-based Daily Scrum focuses on where flow is lacking and what the Developers can do to get it back.
notes.choices:
A) Add a second daily meeting just for blocked items
B) Ask the Scrum Master to unblock the items after the meeting
C) Hold it around the Kanban board and focus on where flow is lacking, such as the blocked items
D) Keep the status round but make it shorter
notes.choicesExplained: A adds an event that Kanban with Scrum does not need. B leaves the Daily Scrum unchanged and moves the blocked items out of it, though a flow-based Daily Scrum asks what the Developers can do about them. D keeps the focus on people instead of flow.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Daily Scrum”, p. 7
notes.evidence: While the goal of the Daily Scrum remains the same as outlined in The Scrum Guide, the meeting itself takes place around the Kanban board and focuses on where flow is lacking and on what actions the Developers can take to get it back.

notes.front: At the Sprint Retrospective, the team wants to understand why items pile up in its “waiting for review” column. What does a flow-based Sprint Retrospective suggest?
notes.back: A) Inspect flow metrics, for example with a cumulative flow diagram, and adapt the Definition of Workflow
notes.explanation: The guide’s flow-based Retrospective inspects flow metrics and adapts the Definition of Workflow, and it names the cumulative flow diagram as a possible aid.
notes.choices:
A) Inspect flow metrics, for example with a cumulative flow diagram, and adapt the Definition of Workflow
B) Wait for the next Sprint Review and ask stakeholders
C) Remove the column from the board so the pile-up disappears
D) Hold a separate Kanban event after the Retrospective
notes.choicesExplained: B moves a process question to an event about the product. C hides the problem instead of inspecting it. D adds an event Kanban with Scrum does not need.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team using Kanban also inspects and adapts the Definition of Workflow to optimize the flow in the next Sprint. Using a cumulative flow diagram to visualize a Scrum Team’s WIP, approximate average Cycle Time and average Throughput can be valuable.

notes.front: A team announces it is “switching from Scrum to Kanban” and will no longer need a Product Owner or Sprint Goals. Using the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams, how should the Scrum Master frame the change?
notes.back: C) Kanban practices enhance and expand Scrum; the Scrum Guide still applies in its entirety
notes.explanation: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams adds to Scrum and assumes the team is operating with the Scrum framework.
notes.choices:
A) Agree: Kanban replaces Scrum’s accountabilities with its own
B) Keep the Product Owner but drop Sprint Goals
C) Kanban practices enhance and expand Scrum; the Scrum Guide still applies in its entirety
D) Adopt Kanban only for work outside the Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: A and B drop parts of Scrum, which the guide says it does not replace. D confines Kanban without reason; its practices can apply inside and outside the Sprint.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Relation to the Scrum Guide”, p. 3
notes.evidence: This guide does not replace or discount any part of The Scrum Guide. It is designed to enhance and expand the practices of Scrum. This guide assumes the reader is operating a process using the Scrum framework. Therefore, The Scrum Guide applies in its entirety.

notes.front: A team has a clear Kanban board and firm WIP limits, yet blocked items sit for days with nobody reacting. Which Kanban practice is the team missing?
notes.back: B) Active management of work items in progress
notes.explanation: The guide says limiting WIP alone is not sufficient, and active management includes responding quickly to blocked work.
notes.choices:
A) Visualisation of the Workflow
B) Active management of work items in progress
C) Limiting WIP
D) Inspecting and adapting the Definition of Workflow
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are already in place: the board is clear and the limits are firm. D adapts policies over time; it is not the day-to-day response to blocked items.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (January 2021), “Active Management of Work Items in Progress”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Limiting WIP is necessary to achieve flow, but it alone is not sufficient. The third practice to establish flow is the active management of work items in progress.
